answer_text:
Assume the usual one-letter-per-envelope interpretation: all \(n!\) bijections from letters to envelopes are equally likely.

Let \(C_i\) be the event that letter \(i\) is placed in envelope \(i\). We want

\[
\Pr(C_1\cup C_2\cup\cdots\cup C_n).
\]

For any fixed set of \(k\) letters, the number of placements in which all those \(k\) letters are in their correct envelopes is \((n-k)!\), since the remaining \(n-k\) letters can be arranged arbitrarily. Thus, for any specific set \(S\) of size \(k\),

\[
\Pr\left(\bigcap_{i\in S} C_i\right)=\frac{(n-k)!}{n!}.
\]

Using the inclusion-exclusion principle, the probability that at least one letter is correct is

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n C_i\right)
&= \sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k+1} \binom{n}{k}\frac{(n-k)!}{n!} \\
&= \sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k+1}\frac{1}{k!}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore the finite-\(n\) probability is

\[
P_n=\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k!}.
\]

Now take the limit as \(n\to\infty\). Since

\[
e^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!},
\]

we have

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n
=
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k!}
=
1-\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}
=
1-\frac{1}{e}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\boxed{
\Pr(\text{at least one correct letter})
=
\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k!}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\Pr(\text{at least one correct letter})
=
1-\frac{1}{e}
}
\]

Numerically, the limiting probability is approximately \(0.6321\).
